question: The rule leaves a hole: when the physics fixes L divisible by four, v2(L) >= 2 on its own and no batch escapes the 4-wide path. Can a masked dummy layer make the layer count odd and give the batch size back control of the width?
mechanism: A layer whose disk mask is all False starts at zero, never changes, and contributes nothing to the layer below -- exactly the free boundary the unpadded lattice has. So L physical layers in an L+1 array is the SAME physics with an odd layer count.

equivalence.note: verified before any timing, since this touches the physics engine

result.verdict: REFUTED as an optimisation. The trick is physically exact and it does restore the lever -- v2(L) goes to 0 so B regains control of the width -- but it loses in all six cells, 10.3% to 27.4%. The arithmetic says why: one extra layer costs 1/L, which is 12.5% at L=8 and 25% at L=4, against a width penalty of 14.3% on an H100. Same order of magnitude, so there is no margin, and the broad sawtooth at +-20% swamps whatever is left.

also: Two design errors of mine. The L=8 lattice has 4232 active sites, between arm A's 2125 (where the width penalty does NOT exist) and arm B's 5245 (where it does), so the saving it was meant to buy may be smaller than the 14.3% measured at 5245. And the H100 has the smallest width penalty of the five devices, so it is the worst place to test a trick that trades traffic for width.
what_remains: For L divisible by four there is no free fix: measure the curve for that geometry and pick the best B. The only route that would cover every geometry is Pallas, where the width becomes ours at no extra traffic.
